prediction with linear models

Fitting the model

Researchers record the rainfall and runoff volumes at a highway location in Texas on 15 different days. Load the measurements:

rain<-read.csv(file="~/Documents/2026F/regression/examples 2103/older/rain.csv")

Take a quick look at the contents of the data:

head(rain)

The data frame has a column called ‘rainfall’ and a column called ‘runoff’.

plot(x=rain$rainfall, y=rain$runoff, 
     xlab="rainfall volume", ylab = "runoff volume")

Fit a linear regression model to estimate the relationship between rainfall volume and runoff volume:

est_model <- lm(runoff~rainfall, data = rain)

Take a look at the model ‘summary’:

summary(est_model)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = runoff ~ rainfall, data = rain)
## 
## Residuals:
##    Min     1Q Median     3Q    Max 
## -8.279 -4.424  1.205  3.145  8.261 
## 
## Coefficients:
##             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept) -1.12830    2.36778  -0.477    0.642    
## rainfall     0.82697    0.03652  22.642  7.9e-12 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 5.24 on 13 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.9753, Adjusted R-squared:  0.9734 
## F-statistic: 512.7 on 1 and 13 DF,  p-value: 7.896e-12

The estimated slope is approximately 0.83, estimated intercept is approx -1.13.

The output above includes two-sided hypothesis tests:

\(H_{0}: \beta_1 = 0 \qquad vs \qquad H_{a}: \beta_{1} \neq 0\)

The hypothesis test for the slope has a very small p value. There is evidence of a non-zero linear relationship between rainfall and runoff.

\[ H_{0}: \beta_{0} = 0 \qquad vs \qquad H_{a}: \beta_{0} \neq 0 \]

The hypothesis test for the intercept, however, has a large p value. With a rejection threshold of 0.05, we would fail to reject the hypothesis that \(\beta_{0}=0\). Based on the observed data, the intercept could be zero.

In context, that does make sense: an intercept of zero would mean there tends to be no water runoff from the highway on days with no rain.

Making predictions

Suppose we want to predict the runoff volume for a day with rainfall of 50.

We could manually construct this from the estimated slope and intercept of the regression line:

## intercept + 50*slope

est_model$coefficients[1] + 50*est_model$coefficients[2]
## (Intercept) 
##    40.22035

We can also use the predict( ) function.

To use the predict( ) function, we specify the name of the model to use to make the predictions, and supply a new data frame containing the x values we want to make predictions for. The x variable in that data frame needs to have the same name as the x variable in the model.

new_rainfall <- data.frame('rainfall'=50)

y_pred <- predict(est_model, newdata = new_rainfall)
print(y_pred)
##        1 
## 40.22035

We can also use the predict( ) function to generate predicted y values for multiple new x values at the same time. Suppose we want to predict the runoff volume for rainfall values 25, 50, and 75:

# to include multiple new x values, we enclose them in c( )

new_rainfall = data.frame('rainfall'=c(25,50,75))

predict(est_model, newdata = new_rainfall)
##        1        2        3 
## 19.54602 40.22035 60.89468

This returns the predicted y value for each of the new x values we specified.

Intervals

Now suppose we’re interested in the average amount of runoff for days with 50 m\(^3\) of rainfall.

The predict( ) function will also give confidence intervals for that quantity.

predict(est_model, newdata= data.frame('rainfall'=50), 
        interval="confidence")
##        fit      lwr      upr
## 1 40.22035 37.28631 43.15439

The output includes the “fitted value” i.e. prediction, and the lower (lwr) and upper (upr) bounds of the confidence interval.

This output tells us that the estimated runoff volume is 40.22, and that we are 95% confident that the true average runoff on days with rainfall of 50 is between 37.3 and 43.2.

By default, this function gives 95% confidence intervals. If we want a different level, we can specify that instead:

predict(est_model, newdata= data.frame('rainfall'=50), 
        interval="confidence", level = 0.99)
##        fit      lwr      upr
## 1 40.22035 36.12932 44.31138

Now the output includes a 99% confidence interval for the average runoff instead of 95%.

Next, suppose we’re interested in the amount of runoff on an individual day with rainfall of 50. We describe this with a “prediction interval” instead of a confidence interval.

The predict( ) function will also give prediction intervals. To get a prediction interval, change the “interval” option:

predict(est_model, newdata= data.frame('rainfall'=50), 
        interval="prediction", level = 0.99)
##        fit      lwr      upr
## 1 40.22035 23.91313 56.52757

We are 99% confident that the runoff volume on an individual day with rainfall of 50 will be between 23.9 and 56.5.

Notice that the 99% prediction interval is wider than the 99% confidence interval. There is more uncertainty about the amount of runoff on an individual day, than about the average across days.

What if we were interested in the amount of runoff on a day with 120m\(^3\) of rainfall, instead?

mean(rain$rainfall)
## [1] 53.2

The average value of rainfall in the sample data was 53.2, close to the value we were considering previously (x=50).

120 is close to the maximum x value in the observed data set, so we are less confident about our ability to make predictions about runoff on days with 120m\(^3\) of rainfall.

predict(est_model, newdata= data.frame('rainfall'=120), 
        interval="confidence", level = 0.95)
##        fit      lwr      upr
## 1 98.10847 92.08128 104.1357

The predicted amount of runoff is 98, and we are 95% confident that on days with rainfall of 120, the true average runoff is between 92 and 104.

The width of this 95% confidence interval is 104 - 92 = 12.

The 95% confidence interval for average runoff on days with rainfall of 50 was 37.3 to 43.2. The width of that interval is only 5.9, much smaller compared to the confidence interval when x=120.

Hypothetically, we could plug in an unreasonably large x value and get a prediction…

predict(est_model, newdata= data.frame('rainfall'=250), 
        interval="confidence", level = 0.95)
##       fit      lwr      upr
## 1 205.615 189.8136 221.4163

A 95% confidence interval for runoff volume on days with rainfall=250 (much larger than the observed values) is approximately 190 to 221. The width of that interval is 31, much larger than either of the previous examples (x=50, x=120).

Simulations (optional section)

We can explore simulations to illustrate the confidence interval for the average y value.

Above, we found the slope and intercept of the estimated regression line for the original data sample.

plot(x=rain$rainfall, y=rain$runoff, xlab="rainfall volume", ylab="runoff volume")
abline(est_model, lwd=3)
legend("bottomright", legend=c("est regression line"), lty=1, col=1, bty='n')
abline(v=50, col="red", lty=2, lwd=3)

With this estimated regression line, the predicted runoff volume on a day with rainfall of 50 was 40.22.

We can imagine collecting a NEW sample of 15 measurements, and fitting a new regression line:

# sample a new 15 measurements from the population
# assuming we have a database of the entire population of measurements
# for purposes of illustration



# choose the points to sample
samples<- sample(1:N, size=15)

# extract their data values
sample_data<-rain_population[samples,]

# fit a regression line to the new sample data
new_model<-lm(runoff ~ rainfall, data= sample_data)

Based on this new sample data, what is our estimate of the runoff when rainfall = 50?

y_pred_new <- predict(new_model, newdata=data.frame('rainfall'=50))
print(y_pred_new)
##        1 
## 40.71664

The prediction is slightly different now.

We can plot the two different estimated regression lines together to illustrate this:

plot(NULL, xlim=c(0,130), ylim=c(0,100), xlab="rainfall volume", ylab="runoff volume")
abline(est_model, lwd=3, col="cornflowerblue")
abline(new_model, lwd=3, col="orange")
legend("bottomright", legend=c("first sample", "second sample" ), lty=1, col=c("cornflowerblue", "orange"), bty='n')
points(x=c(50,50), y=c(y_pred, y_pred_new), cex=1.2, pch=20)

Based on the two different data samples, the point on the regression line for x=50 varies slightly.

Next, imagine taking many different samples of 15 measurements, and fitting a regression line to each of them. Each of those regression lines will have a slightly different y value for x=50.

nrep<-20

# create a data frame full of zeros
# that we can store the intercepts and slopes in
# once we obtain them
# and a vector full of zeros, to store the predicted y values for x=50

regression_coefs<-data.frame('intercept'=rep(0, nrep), 'slope'=rep(0,nrep))

y_preds<-rep(0, length=nrep)


for(i in 1:nrep){
  # draw the new samples
  samples<- sample(1:N, size=15)

  # obtain the rows of the data frame corresponding to those samples
  sample_data<-rain_population[samples,]
  
  # fit regression model
  newmodel<-lm(runoff~rainfall, data=sample_data)
  
  # save the coefficients of the new model
  regression_coefs[i,]<-newmodel$coefficients
  
  # save the prediction for x=50
  
  y_preds[i]<-predict(newmodel, newdata = data.frame('rainfall'=50))
}

The point on the line for x=50 represents our estimate of the average runoff on days with rainfall of 50.

The red dots are the estimated average runoff, estimated in each of the 20 different random data samples.

plot(NULL, xlim=c(0, 100), ylim=c(0, 130), xlab="rainfall", ylab="runoff")
abline(v=50, lty=2, col="gray")
for(i in 1:nrep){
  abline(coef = regression_coefs[i,])
}
points(x=rep(50, nrep), y=y_preds, col="red", pch=20)

We can also zoom in to see the points more clearly:

plot(NULL, xlim=c(45, 55), ylim=c(25, 55), xlab="rainfall", ylab="runoff")
abline(v=50, lty=2, col="gray")
for(i in 1:nrep){
  abline(coef = regression_coefs[i,])
}
points(x=rep(50, nrep), y=y_preds, col="red", pch=20)

The variability in the red dots corresponds to the confidence interval for the true average runoff on a day with rainfall of 50.
